root_cause_summary: The issue was caused by a software defect in Smart Sync's handling of repeated bed connectivity state changes. When a Universal Collector generated multiple rapid Online/Offline status messages for a bed connection, Smart Sync eventually encountered an invalid object type during bed data processing and threw a System.InvalidCastException.

Specifically, Smart Sync attempted to cast a BedConnectorDataNormalizer object to the INormalizeBedData interface, resulting in a processing failure. After this exception occurred, Smart Sync stopped correctly forwarding bed data updates to downstream consumers, causing all bed data to disappear from Status Board. The condition persisted until the Smart Sync service was restarted.

rca_review_comments: A software defect in Smart Sync caused bed data processing to fail when repeated bed disconnect/reconnect events were received from the Universal Collector. Under this condition, Smart Sync encountered an invalid object type conversion, resulting in an unhandled exception that interrupted bed data processing. Once the failure occurred, bed data updates were no longer forwarded to Status Board, causing bed information to disappear until Smart Sync was restarted.

root_cause_summary: The issue was caused by the interaction of two software defects affecting Smart Sync and bed connectivity. First, a change introduced in the GRS5 firmware to support the RCB3 driver increased the frequency of bed disconnections. Second, when a bed disconnected while Smart Sync was actively processing a command, Smart Sync could enter a hung state where its command-processing queue was never cleared, preventing it from processing subsequent bed control messages.

As a result, Patient Safety continued to receive and process staff location events and safety alert suppression events, but bed control commands were no longer being executed. This explains why safety alerts continued to function while bed exit alarm state changes stopped responding. Restarting the Smart Sync service temporarily restored functionality by clearing the blocked processing state.

Reproduction attempts could not recreate beds failing to rearm, but confirmed that restarting the BMS Proxy service while Smart Sync is running always produces a one-second Lost Smart Sync alert, attributed to the SystemAlertProcessor starting before the BedCommController and briefly believing Smart Sync is disconnected. Review also flagged the 1048576 message size quota as too small and easily corrected in a config file; defect NCBL-1862 was created and a related triage defect was referenced for a 4.0.300 fix.

root_cause_summary: When the caregiver left the room, the BMS proxy service and the Smart Sync service were in an errored state and the bed did not rearm automatically.  There was a lost smart sync alert caused by the BMS proxy service restarting just before the caregiver left the room.  Restarting both the BMS Proxy service and the Smart Sync service corrected the issue.
investigation_details: In my testing I have not been able to reproduce the issue with the beds not rearming themselves. Every time I stopped the smart Sync service, simulated the caregiver leaving the room, and then started the smart sync service again, the simulated beds would rearm themselves. I have been able to confirm that anytime the BMS proxy service is Started/Restarted while the smart sync service is running, we will see a 1 second lost smart sync alert. Based on the logs it looks like the caregiver left the room during this one second lost smart sync alert. I believe the one second lost smart sync alerts are caused by BMS Proxy service when the SystemAlertProcessor starts before the BedCommController, briefly the SystemAlertProcessor thinks that the smart sync service is disconnected and makes the lost smart sync alert before the BedCommController can actually subscribe to the smart sync service.
verification_summary: Restarting both the BMS Proxy service and the Smart Sync service corrected the issue.  
Referenced Defect TRIAGE-390 - Fix has been assigned to Voalte Nurse Call 4.0.300.  
BMSProxy service startup has been corrected to no longer generate lost smart sync alert when the service is available.
rca_review_comments: Smart Sync service has a momentary loss in connection when the BMS Proxy Service is restarted, causing the services to not perform NPS actions appropriately until BMS Proxy Service is fully started.

investigation_details: There was a lost secondary console call that could not be cleared by any procedures to clear stuck calls - like marking the call as cancelled in the database and bouncing device service / devices.   I examined the secondary console list for the NUC that was placing the call.   This was RB 5 MB RCB3 NUC (RCB3) - 10.155.66.0 - rcb3-037221Y2WM2.  The nuc’s own ip address appeared in the list, and this was unique for the whole site - no other device had a reference to itself as a secondary.   Looking to see where the list was coming from, I found table function dbo.SecondaryConsoleConfig_GetByOrgUnitId_45.  By running the sql contained in the function, I determined that the reference to itself was coming from a monitoring criteria consisting of only a single room, many call types, and 1 org unit.    This monitoring criteria was somehow orphaned (not deleted or left behind somehow.)   After testing for safety on my machine, I deleted the monitoring criteria with sql statements, pushed configuration, and the lost secondary call disappeared.
troubleshooting_steps: Confirmed correct sw on both RCB and GRS10H. 

Confirmed no call forwarding set for the GRS10H. 

Confirmed no additional monitored units for GRS10H. 

Checked syslogs. No errors for either device. Checked configuration service log. 

Did see some other devices in the syslogs showing the invalid URI lines. 

Confirmed both effected devices are checking in successfully. 

Ran netstat on both devices. Confirmed they successfully establish to each other. 

Performed global push. No change. Purged configuration. No change. 

Forced push sw to both. No change.
troubleshooting_results: The alert makes no sense since the RCB NUC itself is not showing lost. Also the netstat proves the nuc and GRS10h are connected.

summary: NNC Cannot complete ECT save, No device configurations affected message
description: HCA site.  When saving or trying to run global push receive the No device configurations affected message.  Seems to timeout and have looked for timeout settings to allow complete save to no avail.

Requested customer increase memory on SQL server and no response yet.

Had Marva do a check on the DB for indexing issues or any memory concerns.  DB looks to be good shape.

Put Configuration service in Debug mode.  It appears it retries 2-3 times then fails and doesn't successfully complete the task before retrying.
root_cause_summary: The timeout on the ECT was due to the connection timing out between ECT and the configuration service.  The configuration service has very poor performance due to sql in loops that return very small pieces of information.  Also not every column in table functions and scalar functions is indexed.
investigation_details: We requested the customer database for reproduction purposes.  On my machine, configuration would generate and start attempting to push in about 9 minutes and 53 seconds.  There were no devices to push to, so pushing config would fail - this was expected.  Investigating the time consumption, I found the method OrgUnitSettings.GetNursingUnitsForSetup() to be consuming a few seconds every time it was called.  Drilling down into the method, the bottleneck was in the scalar SQL function OrgUnit_HasDisabledNucOrPrimary().  This function is called repeatedly in a loop, and this loop is repeated continuously!  This method joins on two unindexed columns on the device table, and adding an index on these two columns reduced the configuration generation time from 9:53 to 1:53 on my machine.  Going further, I replaced the repeated calls with a strategy of call once and cache the data, this reduced the time further to 1:31.   Creating the index on the customer site allowed configuration to be generated in 3:00.

investigation_details: In the morning on 2/1, I was notified that SDC was down, impacting all production customers. It was discovered that day that the issue was with SDC Mirth’s SQL database. The database had reached 100% utilization in the late evening of 1/31, and as a result new messages were not processing and instead getting queued up. The Dev Ops team increased the size of the database by 1 TB (also on 2/1), and messages began to process in the afternoon.

In the morning on 2/2, I was notified that several customers were reporting ADT messages queueing on their end and not being received by SDC. In SDC, the connection looked fine, and it was not immediately clear that the connection was not functional. After restarting the ADT connection on our end, messages began to come through. All customer connections were redeployed in the morning, which created new queues for the customers. By the afternoon, a majority of these backup queues were depleted, and the system was back to normal. By Sunday, all customers had their backup queues depleted.

description: This issue was reported by HCA JFK Hospital.   When the call table purge job is run nightly at 3:30 am, this causes locking on the call table.   If calls are being updated or inserted into the database at the same time, this will cause the processing of those calls to wait for access to the call table. 

The device service processes all messages on an action block with a parallelism of 1.   When a call insert is being performed and the call table is locked, all other processing will wait, **including heartbeat processing.**  Because the heartbeat timers are still running, they will time out and the device service will drop that socket, **even though wireshark shows heartbeats coming in from the device.**   The recognition of the heartbeat is delayed due to the action block waiting on sql.

1. **Database purge job runs, locking the database's call table.**

    1. Details: The nurse call database purge job runs, which can lock the nurse call database's call table for extended periods (1-2 minutes). 
    
2. **A nurse call is placed.**

    1. Details: Each time a nurse call is placed, the Device Service is responsible for inserting the new call record into the database's call table as part of its standard functionality. investigation_details: When the connector starts (or even when a tag is discovered and the connector is already running or when the connector re-connects), the HPL system will send an initial state of the tag to the rtls connector.  The RTLS connector will receive that message and, because it has a “buttonPress”, it’ll interpret it as a click even though the message also indicates the button press occurred at the beginning of time. So, every time the RTLS Connector disconnects and re-connects to HPL, we’d get one of these mass reporting events; with every single tag that’s assigned at that moment generating a duress call.

HPL does not re-set the timestamp back to `DateTime.MinValue` (ever). So it’ll only be that value if the button has never been clicked. So this fix could get tricky as you’d need to make a decision based on the last time the tag reported. Or something. I’d be happy to rubber duck solution options.

summary: RtlsConnector misinterprets HPL initial-state button info as real-time button events
description: RtlsConnector currently reads `buttonPress` sub-objects from an HPL model update’s `"created"` and/or `"changed"` objects, an interprets them as real-time button events. This results in false button presses sometimes being issued to the nurse call system from HPL, which depending on the configuration may enunciate as invalid duress calls, sometimes in large number at once.
To prevent this, RtlsConnector needs to be modified to only raise button press events if there is one in the `ModelUpdate.Events` collection (`"events"` object).
See https://hill-rom.atlassian.net/browse/RCA-1201 for the history on this topic and more details.
Please reach out to @Matthew Morgan with any questions.
